skills.name: Astronomy
skills.description: From your cosmic address to the edge of the observable universe — the flagship 1–100 tree.

concepts.title: The sky as the first calendar
concepts.description: Ancient cultures tracked the Sun, Moon and stars to mark seasons, plan farming and hold ceremonies.

concepts.title: Andromeda, our big neighbor
concepts.description: Andromeda is the nearest large spiral galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away.

concepts.title: The Apollo Moon landings
concepts.description: Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon during six Apollo landings between 1969 and 1972, bringing back 382 kg of samples.

concepts.title: Asterisms: patterns within constellations
concepts.description: Familiar star patterns like the Big Dipper are asterisms, not official constellations.

concepts.title: The asteroid belt
concepts.description: A wide ring of rocky and metallic asteroids between Mars and Jupiter that never formed a planet.

concepts.title: The astronomical unit
concepts.description: The average Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million km, is the yardstick of the solar system.

concepts.title: The atmosphere gets in the way
concepts.description: Earth’s moving air blurs starlight (stars twinkle) and blocks much of the spectrum, which is why some telescopes go to space.

concepts.title: Binary stars
concepts.description: Many stars orbit partners; watching their orbits lets astronomers weigh stars.

concepts.title: Stars that never set
concepts.description: Stars close to the celestial pole circle it and, from mid-northern latitudes, never dip below the horizon.

concepts.title: Comets
concepts.description: Comets are icy bodies that grow a glowing head and tails when they near the Sun; their tails always point away from it.

concepts.title: Constellation stars aren’t neighbors
concepts.description: Stars in the same constellation are usually at very different distances and only line up from our viewpoint.

concepts.title: What constellations are
concepts.description: Constellations are patterns of stars and, officially, 88 regions that together cover the whole sky.

concepts.title: Dwarf planets and Pluto
concepts.description: In 2006 the IAU defined a planet as clearing its orbital neighborhood; Pluto doesn’t, so it’s a dwarf planet.

concepts.title: A year is one orbit
concepts.description: Earth takes about 365.25 days to orbit the Sun once, moving at about 30 km per second.

concepts.title: What protects life on Earth
concepts.description: Earth’s magnetic field deflects charged particles from the Sun, and its atmosphere and ozone layer shield the surface.

concepts.title: Earth’s spin makes day and night
concepts.description: Earth rotates on its axis about once every 24 hours; the side facing the Sun has day.

concepts.title: Earth is the third planet
concepts.description: Our solar system has eight planets; Earth is the third from the Sun.

concepts.title: The 400× coincidence
concepts.description: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away, so they look the same size.

concepts.title: Solar vs lunar eclipses
concepts.description: A solar eclipse is the Moon blocking the Sun; a lunar eclipse is Earth's shadow falling on the Moon.

concepts.title: The ecliptic
concepts.description: The Sun’s yearly path across the sky; the Moon and planets stay close to it because the solar system is flat.

concepts.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
concepts.description: Visible light is one small band of a spectrum that runs from radio waves to gamma rays; all of it is light traveling at the same speed.

concepts.title: Eratosthenes measures Earth
concepts.description: Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes compared noon shadows in two Egyptian cities to estimate Earth’s circumference.

concepts.title: Escape velocity
concepts.description: To leave Earth completely, a spacecraft must reach about 11.2 km per second.

concepts.title: Galileo’s telescope discoveries
concepts.description: From 1609–1610 Galileo turned a telescope to the sky and found evidence that not everything circles Earth.

concepts.title: The Earth-centered model
concepts.description: For centuries, most scholars placed a motionless Earth at the center, with Ptolemy’s model using small circles (epicycles) to fit planetary motion.

concepts.title: Why an Earth-centered view made sense
concepts.description: We don’t feel Earth moving, and no one could detect stars shifting as Earth orbited.

concepts.title: Gas giants and ice giants
concepts.description: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.

concepts.title: The Sun-centered model
concepts.description: Copernicus placed the Sun at the center, with Earth as one of the planets orbiting it.

concepts.title: The heliosphere
concepts.description: The solar wind blows a bubble around the solar system; Voyager 1 crossed its edge in 2012.

concepts.title: Helium was found in the Sun first
concepts.description: Helium was discovered in the Sun’s spectrum in 1868, before it was found on Earth; its name comes from the Greek word for Sun.

concepts.title: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram
concepts.description: A chart of stars’ luminosity against temperature; most fall on a diagonal band, the main sequence.

concepts.title: The Hubble Space Telescope
concepts.description: Launched in 1990, Hubble orbits above the atmosphere and has made some of astronomy’s sharpest images.

concepts.title: Uranus and Neptune up close
concepts.description: Uranus is tipped on its side; Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system; methane makes both blue.

concepts.title: Infrared astronomy
concepts.description: Infrared light passes through dust, revealing hidden star birth, and captures light from the most distant galaxies.

concepts.title: Jupiter outweighs every other planet combined
concepts.description: Jupiter is the largest planet and has more than twice the mass of all the others put together.

concepts.title: Jupiter’s storms and moons
concepts.description: Jupiter’s Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than Earth; its four large moons are worlds in their own right.

concepts.title: Kepler’s laws
concepts.description: Planets orbit in ellipses, sweep equal areas in equal times, and take longer to orbit the farther out they are.

concepts.title: The Kuiper Belt
concepts.description: A vast ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune, home to Pluto and the source of many comets.

concepts.title: Why leap years exist
concepts.description: The extra quarter-day in each orbit adds up, so the calendar adds a day about every four years.

concepts.title: A light-year is a distance
concepts.description: A light-year is how far light travels in a year: about 9.46 trillion km.

concepts.title: Brightness versus luminosity
concepts.description: How bright a star looks depends on its true output and its distance; brightness fades with the square of distance.

concepts.title: Lunar craters
concepts.description: The Moon’s craters were blasted out by impacts and survive for billions of years because the Moon has no air, water or plate tectonics to erase them.

concepts.title: The Moon’s dark “seas”
concepts.description: The dark patches on the Moon are maria: huge plains of ancient solidified lava, not water.

concepts.title: A star’s mass sets its life
concepts.description: On the main sequence, more massive stars are hotter and brighter but burn out far faster.

concepts.title: Why Mars is red
concepts.description: Mars looks red because iron oxide — rust — coats its dust and rocks.

concepts.title: Mars once had water
concepts.description: Dry river valleys and lake beds show that liquid water once flowed on Mars; today its water is frozen.

concepts.title: Mercury: extremes without air
concepts.description: The smallest planet and closest to the Sun, Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so it swings from scorching days to frigid nights.

concepts.title: Meteoroids, meteors and meteorites
concepts.description: A meteoroid is space debris, a meteor is its streak of light in our sky, and a meteorite is what reaches the ground.

concepts.title: The Milky Way is our galaxy
concepts.description: The Sun is one of more than a hundred billion stars in the Milky Way, a barred spiral galaxy.

concepts.title: The Milky Way is ~100,000 light-years across
concepts.description: Our galaxy is about 100,000 light-years from edge to edge.

concepts.title: The giant-impact origin of the Moon
concepts.description: The leading explanation is that the Moon formed from debris after a Mars-sized body struck the young Earth.

concepts.title: What causes Moon phases
concepts.description: Phases show how much of the Moon's sunlit half faces us; the cycle takes about 29.5 days.

concepts.title: Evidence from Moon rocks
concepts.description: Moon rocks are chemically very similar to Earth’s mantle and the Moon has only a small iron core, consistent with the giant impact.

concepts.title: The Moon always shows us the same face
concepts.description: The Moon is tidally locked: it rotates once per orbit, so the same side always faces Earth.

concepts.title: Each kind of light tells a different story
concepts.description: Astronomers combine radio, infrared, visible, ultraviolet and X-ray views, each revealing different objects.

concepts.title: The nearest star after the Sun
concepts.description: Proxima Centauri, about 4.2 light-years away, is the closest star to the Sun.

concepts.title: Neptune found by mathematics
concepts.description: Irregularities in Uranus’s orbit led astronomers to predict Neptune’s position; it was found there in 1846.

concepts.title: Newton’s law of gravity
concepts.description: One force, universal gravitation, explains falling objects, the Moon’s orbit and Kepler’s laws.

concepts.title: The night sky changes with the seasons
concepts.description: As Earth orbits the Sun, the night side faces different directions in space, so different constellations are visible in different seasons.

concepts.title: Ocean worlds
concepts.description: Some icy moons, like Europa and Enceladus, hide oceans of liquid water beneath their ice, kept liquid by tidal heating.

concepts.title: The Oort Cloud
concepts.description: A vast, distant shell of icy bodies thought to surround the solar system, the source of long-period comets.

concepts.title: An orbit is falling around
concepts.description: A spacecraft in orbit is falling toward Earth but moving sideways so fast that it keeps missing.

concepts.title: Measuring star distances with parallax
concepts.description: Nearby stars shift slightly as Earth orbits; the smaller the shift, the farther the star.

concepts.title: Planets wander against the stars
concepts.description: Planets shift position against the background stars from night to night; “planet” comes from the Greek for wanderer.

concepts.title: The North Star marks north
concepts.description: Polaris sits almost directly above Earth’s North Pole, so it barely moves and marks north.

concepts.title: Earth’s wobble changes the pole star
concepts.description: Earth’s axis slowly wobbles over about 26,000 years, so the pole star changes over millennia.

concepts.title: Radio astronomy
concepts.description: Radio telescopes detect long-wavelength radio waves, which pass through dust and can be observed day and night.

concepts.title: Red giants and planetary nebulae
concepts.description: When a Sun-like star’s core runs low on hydrogen, it swells into a red giant, then sheds its outer layers as a glowing planetary nebula.

concepts.title: Retrograde motion
concepts.description: Planets sometimes appear to move backwards against the stars because Earth overtakes or is overtaken by them.

concepts.title: The four rocky planets
concepts.description: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the small, rocky inner planets.

concepts.title: Ancient scholars knew Earth is round
concepts.description: Greek thinkers had evidence Earth is a sphere, such as its curved shadow on the Moon during lunar eclipses.

concepts.title: Saturn's rings are ice
concepts.description: Saturn's rings are made mostly of chunks of water ice, with some rock.

concepts.title: Seasons aren't about distance
concepts.description: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January — northern winter.

concepts.title: Seasons come from Earth's tilt
concepts.description: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, so each hemisphere takes turns leaning toward the Sun.

concepts.title: Every sky motion has a cause
concepts.description: Daily motion comes from Earth’s spin, yearly changes from Earth’s orbit, and the Moon’s motion and gravity drive phases, eclipses and tides.

concepts.title: Why everything rises in the east
concepts.description: Earth spins west to east, so the Sun, Moon, planets and stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west.

concepts.title: How the solar system formed
concepts.description: About 4.6 billion years ago a spinning cloud of gas and dust collapsed into the Sun and a flat disk that built the planets.

concepts.title: The size of the solar system
concepts.description: The planets span about 30 astronomical units; sunlight takes about 4 hours to reach Neptune.

concepts.title: Solar storms and space weather
concepts.description: The solar wind and eruptions like flares and coronal mass ejections cause auroras and can disrupt technology.

concepts.title: Spectral fingerprints
concepts.description: Each element absorbs and emits its own set of colors, so a spectrum reveals what a star is made of.

concepts.title: Spring and neap tides
concepts.description: When the Sun and Moon line up tides are larger (spring); at right angles they are smaller (neap).

concepts.title: A star's color is its temperature
concepts.description: Blue stars are the hottest; red stars are the coolest.

concepts.title: Where stars are born
concepts.description: Stars form in cold, dense clouds of gas and dust, where gravity pulls clumps together until fusion ignites.

concepts.title: Stars are born, age and die
concepts.description: Stars form in clouds of gas and dust. The Sun will swell into a red giant and end as a white dwarf; massive stars can explode as supernovae.

concepts.title: Navigating by the stars
concepts.description: Before instruments, navigators crossed oceans by memorizing where stars rise and set.

concepts.title: Mass decides a star’s fate
concepts.description: Low-mass stars end as white dwarfs; the most massive leave neutron stars or black holes.

concepts.title: Proof that Earth moves
concepts.description: In 1838 Friedrich Bessel measured stellar parallax, direct evidence that Earth orbits the Sun.

concepts.title: The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old
concepts.description: The Sun formed roughly 4.6 billion years ago.

concepts.title: The Sun runs on nuclear fusion
concepts.description: In its core the Sun fuses hydrogen into helium, releasing the energy that becomes sunlight.

concepts.title: The Sun is a star
concepts.description: The Sun is an ordinary star — the closest one to Earth — not a special category of object.

concepts.title: Inside the Sun
concepts.description: Energy made in the Sun’s core travels out through the radiative and convective zones to the photosphere; the corona above is far hotter.

concepts.title: The Sun holds almost all the mass
concepts.description: About 99.8% of the solar system's mass is in the Sun.

concepts.title: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth
concepts.description: Light from the Sun takes roughly eight minutes to cross the distance to Earth, so we always see the Sun slightly in the past.

concepts.title: Sunspots and the solar cycle
concepts.description: Sunspots are cooler, magnetically active regions whose number rises and falls over an ~11-year cycle.

concepts.title: Supernovae and star stuff
concepts.description: Massive stars explode as supernovae, scattering elements forged inside stars, including those in our bodies.

concepts.title: Bigger is better
concepts.description: A telescope’s light-gathering area sets how faint it can see and how fine the detail it can show.

concepts.title: Refractors and reflectors
concepts.description: Refracting telescopes use lenses; reflecting telescopes use mirrors, and all the largest telescopes are reflectors.

concepts.title: The Moon drives the tides
concepts.description: The Moon’s gravity pulls Earth’s oceans into two bulges, so most coasts get two high tides a day.

concepts.title: Titan
concepts.description: Saturn’s largest moon has a thick nitrogen atmosphere and lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane.

concepts.title: Billions of galaxies, 13.8 billion years
concepts.description: The observable universe holds billions of galaxies and is about 13.8 billion years old.

concepts.title: The discovery of Uranus
concepts.description: William Herschel found Uranus in 1781, the first planet discovered with a telescope.

concepts.title: Venus is the hottest planet
concepts.description: Venus is hotter than Mercury because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat.

concepts.title: Venus: Earth’s twin in size only
concepts.description: Venus is nearly Earth’s size but has crushing pressure, acid clouds and a backwards rotation.

concepts.title: The Voyager probes
concepts.description: Launched in 1977, the twin Voyagers toured the giant planets; Voyager 1 is now in interstellar space.

concepts.title: The James Webb Space Telescope
concepts.description: Launched in 2021, Webb is a huge infrared telescope with a 6.5-meter gold-coated mirror, orbiting the Sun about 1.5 million km from Earth.

concepts.title: White dwarfs
concepts.description: The leftover core of a Sun-like star: about the size of Earth, with much of the Sun’s mass, slowly cooling.

cards.headline: Every star you see at night is a sun. Ours is just the closest one.
cards.body: The Sun isn't a special kind of object. It's a star — the nearest one to Earth. The others only look like dots because they're unimaginably farther away.

cards.headline: Now zoom out much, much further
cards.body: The Sun is one of at least 100 billion stars in the Milky Way, a barred spiral galaxy. That faint band across a dark sky? That's our own galaxy, seen from the inside.

levels.title: The Sun, Up Close
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what powers the Sun and how dominant it is in the solar system.
levels.summary: The Sun fuses hydrogen into helium, holds 99.8% of the solar system's mass, and is about 4.6 billion years old.

cards.headline: The Sun isn't on fire. It's doing something far stranger.
cards.body: There's no burning in the everyday sense. Deep in its core, the Sun squeezes atoms together.

cards.headline: Nuclear fusion
cards.body: At about 15 million °C, the Sun's core squeezes hydrogen atoms so hard that they fuse into helium. Each fusion releases a little energy, and trillions of them every second add up to the sunlight that reaches you.

cards.fact: The Sun holds about 99.8% of the solar system's mass.
cards.context: Every planet, moon, asteroid and comet together makes up the remaining 0.2%. We're the crumbs.

cards.headline: Middle-aged, not old
cards.body: The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago. That sounds ancient, but for a star like ours it's roughly the middle of its life. There's plenty of hydrogen left in its core to keep the fusion going for billions of years more.

levels.summary: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are rocky. Venus is the hottest planet thanks to its heat-trapping atmosphere, and Mars is red because of rust.

cards.headline: Venus: a runaway greenhouse

cards.fact: Mars is red because it's rusty.
cards.context: Iron oxide (the same stuff as rust) coats Martian dust and rocks, and fine red dust in its thin atmosphere tints the whole planet.

levels.title: Why We Have Seasons
levels.objective: After this level you can explain that seasons come from Earth's tilt, not its distance from the Sun.
levels.summary: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. Each hemisphere takes turns leaning toward the Sun, which is why seasons are opposite north and south.

cards.headline: Most people get this one wrong: summer isn't when Earth is closest to the Sun.

cards.fact: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January.
cards.context: That's the middle of winter in the Northern Hemisphere. So distance can't be what makes summer.

cards.headline: It's the tilt
cards.body: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. When your hemisphere leans toward the Sun, sunlight hits the ground more directly and days last longer, so more energy lands on each patch of ground. That's summer. Lean away, and the same sunlight arrives at a slant and spreads thin.

cards.headline: Opposite seasons
cards.body: Because the hemispheres lean opposite ways, December is winter in New York and summer in Sydney. Same planet, same distance, different lean.

options.label: They are pulled toward the Sun’s path by the stars
options.rationale: Distant stars have no such effect.

options.label: Their orbits lie in nearly the same flat plane as Earth’s

options.rationale: Darkness has nothing to do with it.

options.rationale: Planets orbit the Sun, not Earth.

questions.explanation: The solar system is flat: the planets orbit in nearly the same plane as Earth, so from Earth they all appear close to the Sun’s path.

questions.prompt: From Level 7: there’s a new Moon every month. Why isn’t there a solar eclipse every month?

options.label: The Moon is too far away to cover the Sun most months
options.rationale: It’s the tilt of the Moon’s orbit, not its distance, that usually prevents it.

levels.title: Wanderers: How Planets Move Across the Sky
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why planets drift against the stars and sometimes appear to loop backwards.
levels.summary: Planets drift against the stars as they orbit. When Earth overtakes an outer planet, it seems to go backwards: retrograde motion.

cards.headline: Every few years, Mars seems to stop, reverse and loop back across the sky.
cards.body: It never actually turns around. You’re watching from a moving planet.

cards.headline: The wanderers
cards.body: Night after night, the stars keep the same patterns. Planets don’t: they slowly shift position against the background stars as they orbit the Sun. The ancient Greeks noticed, and the word “planet” comes from their word for “wanderer.”

cards.headline: Overtaking on the inside lane
cards.body: Earth orbits closer to the Sun than Mars does, so it moves faster. When Earth catches up with Mars and passes it, Mars appears to slide backwards against the stars for a few weeks, then forward again. It’s like passing a slower car: it seems to drift backwards, though both are going forward.

cards.fact: Retrograde motion is only apparent.
cards.context: No planet ever reverses direction in its orbit. The backwards loop is a change in our viewpoint, not in the planet’s path.

cards.headline: Wanderers: explained
learned: Planets drift against the stars as they orbit

Retrograde motion is only apparent

options.label: Wanderer
Child of the Sun
options.rationale: That’s not the word’s origin.

questions.explanation: Planets drift against the fixed patterns of stars, so the Greeks called them “wanderers.”

options.rationale: Planets never reverse; this is an illusion.

levels.title: Tides: The Moon’s Pull on the Ocean
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why most coasts get two high tides a day and what spring and neap tides are.
levels.summary: The Moon’s gravity makes two bulges of ocean water. Earth spins through both each day; the Sun makes tides bigger or smaller.

cards.headline: The Moon moves oceans. Twice a day.
Two bulges, not one
cards.body: The Moon’s gravity pulls on Earth’s oceans, stretching them into two bulges: one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side of Earth. As Earth spins, most coastlines pass through both bulges, getting two high tides and two low tides about every 24 hours and 50 minutes.

cards.headline: The Sun joins in
cards.body: The Sun pulls on the oceans too, more weakly. Around new and full Moon, the Sun, Moon and Earth line up and their pulls combine into extra-high and extra-low tides: spring tides. Around the quarter Moons they pull at right angles and tides are gentler: neap tides.

cards.fact: Spring tides have nothing to do with spring.
cards.context: They happen twice a month, all year round. The name comes from water “springing” up higher.

cards.headline: Tides: explained
learned: The Moon’s gravity makes two ocean bulges

Neap tides: Sun and Moon at right angles

options.label: The Sun’s heat

options.label: The Moon orbits Earth twice every single day
options.rationale: The Moon orbits once a month.

options.label: Earth spins through two tidal bulges each day

options.label: The Sun, Earth and Moon are in a line

questions.explanation: At new Moon the Moon is between Earth and the Sun; at full Moon, Earth is between them. Either way they line up, and their pulls add up.

levels.title: Where the Moon Came From
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the giant-impact explanation for the Moon’s origin and the evidence for it.
levels.summary: The Moon most likely formed from debris after a Mars-sized body hit the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago.

cards.headline: The Moon may be made of pieces of Earth.
cards.body: The leading explanation starts with one of the biggest collisions in the solar system’s history.

cards.headline: The giant impact
cards.body: About 4.5 billion years ago, soon after Earth formed, a Mars-sized body (scientists call it Theia) is thought to have slammed into it. The crash threw huge amounts of molten rock into orbit, and that debris gathered to form the Moon.

cards.headline: The clues
cards.body: Rocks brought back by Apollo astronauts are chemically very similar to rocks from Earth’s mantle, the layer below the crust. And the Moon has only a small iron core, which fits a Moon built mostly from rocky outer layers rather than Earth’s iron heart. Computer simulations of such a collision can produce exactly this kind of Moon.

cards.headline: Moon origin: reconstructed
learned: The Moon likely formed from a giant impact
A Mars-sized body (Theia) hit the young Earth
That was about 4.5 billion years ago
Moon rocks closely match Earth’s mantle

options.label: It drifted in from another star system

levels.title: Craters and Seas on the Moon
levels.objective: After this level you can explain where lunar craters and the dark “seas” came from and why they last so long.
levels.summary: Craters are impact scars preserved for billions of years; the dark maria are ancient hardened lava.

cards.headline: The “Man in the Moon” is made of ancient lava.
Scars that never heal
cards.body: The Moon’s craters were blasted out by asteroids and comets, and range from tiny pits to basins hundreds of kilometers wide. On Earth, wind, rain and shifting plates wear craters away. The Moon has almost no atmosphere, no liquid water and no plate tectonics, so its craters survive for billions of years.
cards.callout: No air, no water, no erasing

cards.headline: Seas without water
cards.body: The dark patches are called maria, Latin for “seas,” because early astronomers thought they might be water. They’re actually vast plains of ancient lava that flooded low areas and hardened. Most of them are on the near side, the side that faces Earth.

cards.headline: Lunar surface: surveyed
learned: Craters come from asteroid and comet impacts
No air, water or plate tectonics erase them
Maria are plains of ancient hardened lava
Most maria are on the near side

options.label: Shadows of mountains

options.rationale: Sunlight reaches them like the rest of the surface.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Reading the Sky
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the everyday motions of the Sun, Moon, stars and planets and the tides they cause.
levels.summary: Spin makes days, orbits make years and seasons, and the Moon’s orbit and gravity drive phases, eclipses and tides.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale. Everything in the sky moves for a reason.
cards.body: You now know the reason for almost all of it. Let’s put it together.

cards.headline: Spin, orbit, pull
cards.body: Earth’s spin gives day and night and sweeps the stars across the sky. Its orbit gives the year, the seasons and a changing night sky. And the Moon, circling us, brings phases, eclipses and tides.
cards.callout: Spin → day · Orbit → year · Moon → tides

cards.fact: Each star rises about 4 minutes earlier every night.
cards.context: Earth moves a little along its orbit each day, so the stars get a head start. Over a year those minutes add up to a whole different night sky.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 complete
learned: Earth’s spin: day, night and a turning sky
Earth’s orbit: the year and a changing night sky
The Moon: phases, eclipses and tides

levels.title: The First Sky-Watchers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how ancient cultures used the sky to keep calendars and navigate.
levels.summary: The sky was humanity’s first calendar and map: monuments, floods, eclipses and ocean voyages were all timed by it.

cards.headline: Long before clocks, the sky was the clock.
cards.body: The same patterns you learned in Chapter 2 ran farming, festivals and voyages for thousands of years.

cards.headline: Calendars in stone and stars
cards.body: Stonehenge in England lines up with the midsummer sunrise and the midwinter sunset. In ancient Egypt, the first dawn appearance of the star Sirius each year was linked with the Nile’s annual flood, which made the farmland fertile.

cards.headline: Records that predicted the sky
cards.body: Babylonian astronomers kept careful records of the Moon and planets on clay tablets. Over generations those records revealed repeating patterns, and they used them to predict eclipses.

cards.fact: Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of kilometers of open ocean without instruments.
cards.context: They memorized where stars rise and set on the horizon, and read ocean swells and birds, to steer between islands.

cards.headline: Ancient astronomy: discovered

levels.title: Eratosthenes Measures the Earth
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a shadow and a well let someone estimate Earth’s size over 2,000 years ago.
levels.summary: Comparing the noon Sun in two cities, Eratosthenes estimated Earth’s circumference remarkably well around 240 BCE.

cards.headline: Around 240 BCE, someone measured the whole Earth without leaving Egypt.
Two cities, one Sun
cards.body: Eratosthenes heard that at Syene, at noon on the summer solstice, the Sun shone straight down a deep well. At the same moment in Alexandria, farther north, a vertical pole cast a shadow about 7° from vertical, roughly one-fiftieth of a full circle.

cards.headline: From angle to planet
cards.body: If Earth is a sphere, the angle difference means the distance between the cities is one-fiftieth of the way around the globe. Multiply that distance by 50 and you get Earth’s circumference. His answer was remarkably close to the modern value of about 40,000 km.

cards.fact: Greek thinkers already knew Earth was round.
cards.context: During lunar eclipses, Earth’s shadow on the Moon is always curved, the shape only a sphere casts every time.

cards.headline: Earth: measured

levels.title: An Earth-Centered Universe
levels.objective: After this level you can describe the geocentric model and why it lasted for more than a thousand years.
levels.summary: Ptolemy’s Earth-centered model used epicycles to match the planets and lasted about 1,400 years.

cards.headline: For 1,400 years, scholars agreed: Earth sits still at the center.
cards.body: It wasn’t a foolish idea. It fit what people could actually see.

cards.headline: Ptolemy’s universe
cards.body: Around 150 CE, Ptolemy described a model with Earth motionless at the center and the Sun, Moon, planets and stars circling it. To match the planets’ loops, each planet rode on a small circle, an epicycle, that itself moved around Earth. Complicated, yes, but it matched what people saw.

cards.headline: Why it made sense
cards.body: You can’t feel Earth moving. And if Earth orbited the Sun, nearby stars should shift slightly over a year. Nobody could detect such a shift, called parallax, which seemed to prove Earth stood still. The model also predicted planet positions well enough to be useful.

cards.headline: Geocentric model: understood
learned: Ptolemy put a motionless Earth at the center
Epicycles explained the planets’ loops
No one could feel Earth move or see stellar parallax
The model lasted about 1,400 years

levels.title: Copernicus Moves the Sun
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the heliocentric model and why it explained retrograde motion more simply.
levels.summary: In 1543 Copernicus put the Sun at the center, making Earth just another planet and explaining retrograde loops naturally.

cards.headline: In 1543, one book quietly demoted Earth to “just another planet.”
The Sun in the middle
cards.body: Nicolaus Copernicus published a model with the Sun at the center and Earth as one of several planets orbiting it. Earth’s daily spin explained the turning sky; its yearly orbit explained the Sun’s path through the stars.

cards.headline: Loops without epicycles
cards.body: In this model, retrograde motion is simply Earth overtaking the outer planets. No extra circles are needed to cause it. Copernicus still assumed perfectly circular orbits, though, so his model needed some small circles of its own to match observations.

cards.fact: Copernicus wasn’t the first.
cards.context: Aristarchus of Samos proposed a Sun-centered arrangement around 1,800 years earlier, but the idea didn’t catch on.

cards.headline: Heliocentric model: understood
learned: Copernicus published a Sun-centered model in 1543
Earth became one of the planets

questions.explanation: With the Sun at the center, retrograde loops follow naturally from Earth passing the outer planets.

levels.summary: Galileo’s telescope revealed moons circling Jupiter, a full set of Venus phases, lunar mountains and a starry Milky Way.

cards.headline: In 1610, four tiny moons around Jupiter cracked the Earth-centered universe.
Borrowed idea, better instrument
cards.body: Galileo didn’t invent the telescope; it first appeared in the Netherlands in 1608. But he built better ones and, in 1609, pointed them at the sky. He found mountains and craters on the Moon and saw that the Milky Way is made of countless stars.

cards.headline: Moons that don’t orbit Earth
cards.body: Galileo found four moons circling Jupiter: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. Here was proof that not everything circles Earth.

cards.fact: Venus has phases, just like the Moon.
cards.context: Galileo saw Venus go through a full set of phases, from crescent to nearly full. Ptolemy’s model couldn’t produce that; a Venus orbiting the Sun could.

levels.title: Kepler’s Ellipses
levels.objective: After this level you can state Kepler’s laws in plain words and explain why planets speed up near the Sun.
levels.summary: Using Tycho Brahe’s data, Kepler found that orbits are ellipses, planets speed up near the Sun, and outer planets take longer.

cards.headline: Planets don’t move in circles. Proving it took the best data of the age.
Ellipses, not circles
cards.body: Johannes Kepler studied the precise naked-eye observations of Tycho Brahe. Circles never quite fit Mars. Ellipses did. His first law: planets orbit the Sun in ellipses, with the Sun at one focus rather than the center.

cards.headline: Faster when closer
cards.body: His second law says a line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. In practice, a planet moves fastest when it’s closest to the Sun and slowest when farthest. His third law adds that the farther out a planet orbits, the longer its year.
cards.callout: Law 2: faster near the Sun · Law 3: farther = longer year

levels.title: Newton’s Gravity
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how one law of gravity covers falling apples, orbiting moons and planets.
levels.summary: Newton’s universal gravitation (1687) showed one force governs falling objects, the Moon and the planets, explaining Kepler’s laws.

cards.headline: The force that drops an apple also holds the Moon in the sky.
One law for everything
cards.body: In 1687 Isaac Newton published his law of universal gravitation. Every object pulls on every other. The pull grows with their masses and weakens with the square of the distance: twice as far, a quarter of the pull. On the Moon, surface gravity is only about one-sixth of Earth’s, so you would weigh about one-sixth as much there.

cards.headline: Heaven and Earth, united
cards.body: Newton showed that the gravity making things fall on Earth also keeps the Moon in orbit and the planets circling the Sun. His law explained why Kepler’s laws work, turning a description into an explanation.

levels.title: Measuring the Solar System
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the astronomical unit and how astronomers measured the size of the solar system.
levels.summary: Kepler gave the solar system’s shape; transits of Venus and later radar gave its size: 1 AU ≈ 150 million km.

cards.headline: Knowing the shape of the solar system isn’t the same as knowing its size.
A map without a scale
cards.body: Kepler’s laws told astronomers the relative distances of the planets: Mars is about 1.5 times farther from the Sun than Earth, for example. But without one real distance in kilometers, the map had no scale. Every distance in the solar system depended on that one missing number.

cards.headline: Chasing Venus
cards.body: In 1761 and 1769, astronomers spread around the world to time Venus crossing the face of the Sun. Comparing their views let them work out the Earth–Sun distance. Today radar and spacecraft pin it down very precisely.

cards.fact: 1 astronomical unit (AU) is about 150 million km.
cards.context: It’s the average Earth–Sun distance, and the solar system’s standard yardstick.

levels.title: New Planets: Uranus and Neptune
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Uranus was found by telescope and Neptune was predicted by mathematics.
levels.summary: Herschel spotted Uranus in 1781. Tugs on Uranus’s orbit let Le Verrier predict Neptune, found in 1846 almost exactly where predicted.

cards.headline: One planet was found with a telescope. The next was found with a pencil.
A planet no one had seen
cards.body: In 1781, William Herschel spotted a slow-moving object that turned out to be a new planet: Uranus. It was the first planet discovered with a telescope. Every planet out to Saturn had been known since ancient times. Uranus is so faint that earlier astronomers had recorded it and mistaken it for a star.

cards.headline: Found by mathematics
cards.body: Uranus didn’t quite follow its predicted path, as if something unseen were tugging it. Using Newton’s gravity, Urbain Le Verrier calculated where that unseen planet should be. In 1846 Johann Galle looked there and found Neptune, within about a degree of the prediction.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How We Know
levels.objective: After this level you can trace how observation and reasoning moved humanity from an Earth-centered sky to modern astronomy.
levels.summary: From Eratosthenes to Bessel, better observations kept testing ideas, until stellar parallax proved that Earth moves.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale. The last ancient objection falls.
cards.body: For 2,000 years, no one could see the stars shift as Earth moved. Then someone did.

events.label: Copernicus puts the Sun at the center

cards.context: The star, 61 Cygni, moved by a tiny angle over the year: the first measured distance to a star, and direct proof that Earth goes around the Sun, as Copernicus had argued.

levels.title: More Than Meets the Eye: The Spectrum
levels.objective: After this level you can explain that visible light is one small part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
levels.summary: Radio waves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all light, differing only in wavelength.

cards.headline: Your eyes are missing almost everything.
cards.body: Most of the light in the universe is invisible to us. Astronomers have learned to see it anyway.

cards.headline: One spectrum, many names
cards.body: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all the same thing: light. What makes them different is wavelength. Radio waves are the longest, gamma rays the shortest, and visible light is a thin sliver in between.

cards.headline: Same speed, every kind
cards.body: Every kind of light, from radio to gamma rays, crosses space at the speed of light. Within the visible band, the colors are wavelengths too: red is the longest and violet the shortest.

cards.fact: Human eyes see only wavelengths from about 380 to 700 nanometers.
cards.context: Anything longer, like infrared, or shorter, like ultraviolet, is invisible to us. Some animals, such as bees, can see ultraviolet.

levels.title: Starlight’s Fingerprints
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how spectra reveal what stars are made of.
levels.summary: Each element leaves its own lines in a spectrum, so starlight reveals what stars are made of: mostly hydrogen and helium.

cards.headline: We know what stars are made of without ever touching one.
Lines like barcodes
cards.body: Spread starlight into a rainbow and you’ll find thin dark lines crossing it. Each chemical element absorbs and emits light only at its own set of wavelengths, so each makes its own pattern of lines, like a barcode.

cards.headline: Reading a star
cards.body: By matching the lines in a star’s spectrum to elements measured in the lab, astronomers can tell what the star contains. The answer, for almost every star: mostly hydrogen and helium.

cards.fact: Helium was discovered in the Sun before it was found on Earth.
cards.context: In 1868 astronomers saw an unknown line in the Sun’s spectrum. The new element was named after Helios, the Greek word for the Sun.

cards.headline: A telescope is a light bucket. Bigger bucket, more universe.
Lenses or mirrors
cards.body: Refracting telescopes, like Galileo’s, gather light with lenses. Reflecting telescopes gather it with curved mirrors. Isaac Newton built the first practical reflector in 1668.

cards.headline: Why size matters
cards.body: A wider mirror or lens collects more light, so it can see fainter objects and show finer detail. That’s why astronomers keep building bigger telescopes. All the largest are reflectors: a huge lens would sag under its own weight, but a mirror can be supported from behind.

cards.fact: The biggest optical telescopes today have mirrors about 10 meters across.
cards.context: Mirrors that size are built from many smaller segments fitted together. Telescopes with mirrors more than 30 meters wide are already under construction.

cards.headline: Twinkling is beautiful. For astronomers, it’s a problem.
The trouble with air
cards.body: Stars twinkle because moving pockets of air bend their light back and forth, blurring what telescopes see. The atmosphere also blocks most ultraviolet light and X-rays, and much infrared, from ever reaching the ground.

cards.headline: Hubble, above it all
cards.body: The Hubble Space Telescope launched in 1990 and orbits above the atmosphere, so its images are free of that blurring. It’s also the only space telescope designed to be repaired and upgraded by astronauts in orbit.

cards.fact: Hubble helped measure the age of the universe.
cards.context: Its sharp observations of distant galaxies helped pin the universe’s age at about 13.8 billion years, a number you met back in Level 10.

levels.title: Listening to the Sky: Radio Astronomy
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what radio telescopes detect and why they are so large.
levels.summary: Radio telescopes catch long radio waves that pierce dust and work day or night. Linked dishes act like one giant telescope.

cards.headline: Some telescopes don’t need darkness. They work at noon, through clouds.
A new window
cards.body: In the early 1930s, Karl Jansky picked up radio waves coming from the Milky Way. Radio astronomy was born. Radio waves pass through cosmic dust and Earth’s clouds, and radio telescopes can observe in daylight.

cards.headline: Why the dishes are huge
cards.body: Radio waves are very long, so seeing fine detail takes an enormous dish. Astronomers go further by linking many dishes into arrays that work together like one much larger telescope.

cards.fact: The Very Large Array in New Mexico links 27 radio dishes.
cards.context: Spread out over up to 36 km, they work together like a single dish of that size, sharp enough to map the radio sky in fine detail.

cards.headline: Pluto didn’t change in 2006. The definition of a planet did.
Three tests for a planet

cards.headline: The solar system’s true edge may be a shell of ice no one has ever seen.
A giant shell
cards.body: The Oort Cloud is thought to be a giant spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the whole solar system, perhaps reaching 100,000 astronomical units from the Sun. That’s about 100,000 times the Earth–Sun distance.

cards.headline: Known only from comets
cards.body: No object has ever been seen in the Oort Cloud itself. Astronomers infer it from comets that take thousands of years or more to orbit the Sun: their paths trace back to a distant shell all around us.

cards.fact: Voyager 1 will take about 300 years to reach its inner edge.
cards.context: And that’s the fastest-moving, most distant spacecraft we have.

Dark, but not cold

cards.headline: The Sun has weather, and it reaches all the way to us.

cards.headline: When storms arrive
cards.body: When those particles reach Earth, our magnetic field steers many of them toward the poles, where they make the sky glow as auroras. Strong storms can also disrupt satellites, radio communications and power grids.

cards.fact: The Carrington Event of 1859 is the strongest solar storm on record.
cards.context: It produced auroras seen far from the poles. A storm like it today could seriously disrupt technology.

levels.title: How the Solar System Formed
levels.objective: After this level you can outline how the Sun and planets formed from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust.
levels.summary: A collapsing, spinning cloud flattened into a disk: the Sun at its center, rocky planets inside the frost line, giants outside.

cards.headline: Every planet, moon and comet began as part of one cloud.
A spinning cloud collapses
cards.body: About 4.6 billion years ago, a cloud of gas and dust began collapsing under its own gravity. As it shrank it spun faster and flattened into a disk, with the young Sun forming at the center. That’s why the planets still orbit in nearly the same plane.

cards.headline: The frost line
cards.body: Close to the young Sun it was too hot for ices to form, so only rock and metal could clump into planets: small, rocky worlds. Farther out, beyond the frost line, ices could condense too. With far more material to build from, the giant planets grew huge.

levels.title: Checkpoint: The Sun’s Domain

levels.summary: The solar wind blows a bubble, the heliosphere, around the planets. Voyager 1 crossed its edge in 2012.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale. Where does the solar system actually end?
cards.body: It depends on what you measure: the planets, the solar wind, or the Sun’s gravity.

cards.headline: The Sun’s bubble
cards.body: The solar wind blows a vast bubble around the Sun and planets called the heliosphere. Its outer edge, the heliopause, is where the solar wind gives way to interstellar space. Voyager 1 crossed it in 2012.

cards.headline: But gravity reaches farther

levels.title: Parallax: Measuring the Stars
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how parallax measures the distance to nearby stars.
levels.summary: Nearby stars shift slightly as Earth orbits; the smaller the shift, the farther the star. Gaia has measured over a billion.

cards.headline: Blink one eye, then the other. That jump is how we measure the stars.
cards.body: Hold a finger in front of your face and it seems to hop against the background. Stars do the same as Earth moves.

cards.headline: A six-month baseline
cards.body: As Earth orbits the Sun, a nearby star appears to shift slightly against more distant stars. Measure the star in January and again in July, from opposite sides of Earth’s orbit, and that tiny shift reveals its distance.

cards.headline: Closer shifts more
cards.body: The closer a star is, the bigger its parallax shift. Astronomers even named a unit after it: a parsec, the distance at which the shift would be one arcsecond, is about 3.26 light-years.

cards.fact: The Gaia spacecraft has measured more than a billion stars.
cards.context: This European Space Agency mission has mapped the positions and distances of stars across our galaxy using parallax.

Two kinds of bright

cards.headline: Fading with distance
cards.body: A star’s brightness falls with the square of its distance. Move a star twice as far away and it looks only a quarter as bright; ten times as far, a hundredth.

levels.summary: Plot stars by luminosity and temperature and a pattern appears: the main sequence, with giants above and white dwarfs below.

cards.headline: Put every star on one chart and a hidden pattern jumps out.
Luminosity versus temperature
cards.body: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram plots stars by how luminous they are and how hot their surfaces are. It’s named after Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell, who developed it independently in the early 1900s.

cards.headline: Where the stars fall
cards.body: Most stars fall along a diagonal band called the main sequence, and the Sun sits near its middle: a thoroughly average star. Red giants sit in the upper right: cool but very luminous. White dwarfs sit in the lower left: hot but dim. A star’s place on the chart tells you what stage of life it’s in.

levels.title: The Main Sequence
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a star’s mass decides its temperature and lifetime.
levels.summary: Main-sequence stars fuse hydrogen. The most massive burn out in millions of years; red dwarfs can last trillions.

cards.headline: Life on the main sequence
cards.body: A main-sequence star is fusing hydrogen into helium in its core. Stars spend most of their lives this way, which is why most stars on the H–R diagram fall on the main sequence. The Sun will spend about 10 billion years there in total.

cards.headline: Mass sets the pace
cards.body: A more massive star has a hotter, denser core, so it fuses its fuel much faster. It shines hotter and brighter, but the most massive stars last only a few million years. The smallest, red dwarfs, use fuel so slowly they can shine for trillions of years.
cards.callout: More mass → hotter, brighter, shorter life

cards.fact: Our nearest stellar neighbor is a red dwarf.
cards.context: Proxima Centauri is small, cool and dim, far too faint to see without a telescope, but it will outlive the Sun by an enormous margin.

cards.headline: Weighing stars

levels.title: Stellar Nurseries
levels.objective: After this level you can describe how stars form inside nebulae.
levels.summary: Stars form in cold, dense clouds of gas and dust. The Orion Nebula, 1,300 light-years away, is the nearest big nursery.

cards.headline: Stars are being born right now, and you can see one nursery yourself.
From cloud to star
cards.body: Stars form inside cold, dense clouds of gas and dust. Gravity pulls clumps of the cloud together. As a clump shrinks, its center gets hotter and denser, until it’s hot enough for fusion to begin. A star is born.

cards.headline: The nearest nursery
cards.body: The Orion Nebula, about 1,300 light-years away, is the nearest large region of star formation. Look at the sword hanging from Orion’s belt on a dark night and you’ll see it as a fuzzy patch.

cards.fact: Hubble photographed the “Pillars of Creation” in 1995.
cards.context: These towering columns of gas and dust in the Eagle Nebula are full of forming stars, one of the most famous images in astronomy.

levels.title: Red Giants and Planetary Nebulae
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Sun-like stars swell and shed their outer layers.
levels.summary: When the core runs low on hydrogen, a Sun-like star swells into a red giant, then puffs off its outer layers as a planetary nebula.

cards.headline: Someday the Sun will swallow Mercury and Venus.
Swelling up
cards.body: When a Sun-like star’s core runs low on hydrogen, the core contracts and heats up while the star’s outer layers swell enormously. It becomes a red giant. The Sun is expected to grow large enough to engulf Mercury and Venus, and possibly Earth.

cards.headline: A glowing farewell
cards.body: Late in life, a Sun-like star sheds its outer layers into space as a glowing shell of gas called a planetary nebula. Despite the name, it has nothing to do with planets: early astronomers thought these round glows looked like planets’ disks through small telescopes. Each one glows for only tens of thousands of years.

levels.title: White Dwarfs
levels.objective: After this level you can describe white dwarfs and why they slowly cool.
levels.summary: A white dwarf is a dead star’s core: Earth-sized, nearly Sun-massive, so dense a teaspoon weighs tons, and slowly cooling.

cards.headline: A teaspoon of this star would weigh several tons.
A star-sized core in an Earth-sized ball
cards.body: After shedding its outer layers, a Sun-like star leaves behind its exposed core: a white dwarf. It’s about the size of Earth, but with a mass comparable to the Sun’s. That makes it incredibly dense: a teaspoonful would weigh several tons on Earth.

cards.headline: Slowly fading
cards.body: A white dwarf no longer fuses anything. It shines only with its leftover heat and slowly cools over billions of years. The nearest example is Sirius B, the faint partner of the brightest star in the sky. Most stars in our galaxy, the Sun included, will end this way.

levels.title: Supernovae and Star Stuff
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how massive stars explode and scatter the elements we are made of.
levels.summary: Stars over ~8 Suns’ mass end in core-collapse supernovae, spreading the elements forged in stars, including those in us.

cards.headline: The iron in your blood was made inside a star.
Going out with a bang
cards.body: Stars more than about eight times as massive as the Sun end their lives when their cores collapse. The collapse triggers a supernova, an explosion that can briefly outshine an entire galaxy.

cards.headline: Cosmic recycling
cards.body: Nearly all the elements heavier than hydrogen and helium were made by nuclear reactions inside stars and in stellar explosions. Supernovae scatter them into space, where they become part of new stars, planets and people. The calcium in your bones was forged in stars that died before the Sun formed.

cards.fact: In 1987, a supernova was visible to the naked eye.
cards.context: It exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy near the Milky Way: the closest supernova seen in centuries.

levels.title: Checkpoint: The Lives of Stars
levels.objective: After this level you can trace a star’s life from nebula to its final state based on its mass.
levels.summary: Mass decides everything: Sun-like stars end as white dwarfs, while the most massive leave neutron stars or black holes.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale. One number decides a star’s whole life story.
cards.body: That number is its mass.

cards.headline: Two paths
cards.body: A star’s final fate depends mainly on its mass. A Sun-like star swells into a red giant, sheds a planetary nebula and ends as a white dwarf. A star far more massive than the Sun explodes as a supernova and leaves behind something much stranger: a neutron star or a black hole.
